title: Tiny Lamb Dumplings with Garlic Yoghurt and Paprika Butter
summary: More than a hundred pinches become tiny pyramids of thin dough filled with spiced minced lamb, boiled until tender and served over garlic yoghurt with a brick-red paprika butter, dried mint and sumac.
equipment: ruler and sharp knife or pizza wheel
2 floured trays and a clean tea towel

ingredients.item: plain flour, plus extra for dusting
fine sea salt or table salt
small onion, coarsely grated, juice squeezed out
fine sea salt or table salt
fine sea salt or table salt
Aleppo pepper (pul biber) or sweet paprika

steps.title: Knead the dough
steps.text: Mix the flour and dough salt in the large bowl, make a well and add the egg and 90 ml water. Stir with a fork, then bring together by hand, adding 1 tbsp more water only if dry flour remains. Knead for 8 min until smooth and firm, then cover and rest for 30 min. A firm, well-kneaded dough can be rolled very thin without tearing.

steps.title: Mix the filling
steps.text: Combine the lamb, squeezed onion, parsley, filling salt, pepper and paprika and work with your hands for about 1 min until sticky. Squeezing the onion keeps the filling from going watery, and the sticky texture helps it hold together inside the dough. Cover and chill, and wash your hands after handling raw meat.

steps.title: Season the yoghurt
steps.text: Stir the yoghurt, garlic and yoghurt salt together and leave at room temperature while you work, for up to 1 h. Taking the chill off means it will not cool the hot dumplings too much when served.

steps.title: Roll and cut
steps.text: Cut the dough into 4, keeping the rest covered. Roll one piece on a lightly floured surface as thin as you can, about 1 mm, into a rough 30 cm square, then cut into 5 cm squares, 36 per sheet. Thin dough cooks quickly and evenly, matching the small amount of filling.

steps.title: Fold the pyramids
steps.text: Place a chickpea-sized piece of filling (about 2.5 g) in the centre of each square. Bring the four corners up over the filling and pinch the four seams together to seal into a little pyramid, then set on a floured tray. Repeat with the remaining dough; you should get about 140, which uses up the filling.

steps.title: Boil and probe
steps.text: Bring a large pan of unsalted water to the boil, add half the manti and stir gently once. Simmer for 6-8 min after they rise to the surface, until the dough is tender, including the pinched tops. Cut one open: the filling should be cooked through everywhere and read 71°C in the centre with the probe. Lift out with the slotted spoon into a warm dish and repeat with the rest.

steps.title: Make the paprika butter
steps.text: While the second batch cooks, melt the butter in the small saucepan over medium heat until it foams. Stir in the tomato paste and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30-60 s until brick red and fragrant, then add the 2 tbsp water and take off the heat. Frying the paste briefly deepens its flavour, and the water stops the butter overheating.

steps.title: Assemble and serve
steps.text: Spread the garlic yoghurt in 4 shallow bowls and pile the hot manti on top. Spoon over the paprika butter, sprinkle with the dried mint and sumac and serve straight away.

tips: A common mistake is leaving the dough too thick; roll it to about 1 mm, or the pinched tops stay doughy after cooking.
Pinch the seams firmly so the parcels stay sealed in the simmering water.
Squeeze the grated onion well, as extra juice makes the filling loose and hard to portion.
Keep the shaped manti covered with the tea towel so they do not dry and crack.
storage: Refrigerate manti and sauces separately within 2 hours for up to 2 days; reheat the manti in a covered pan with a splash of water until piping hot (74°C). Freeze uncooked manti on a tray and boil from frozen, adding 2-3 min.
